To exasperate someone means to make them feel intensely frustrated, annoyed, and completely out of patience — particularly through behavior that is repeated, ongoing, or impossible to easily stop.

It's importantly stronger than just "annoy" or "bother." When you exasperate someone, you push them to the very edge of their patience. They don't feel a little irritated — they feel emotionally worn out, like they've had enough and can't take it anymore.

Picture this: someone pokes you once. Annoying. They poke you ten times in a row, and you throw your hands up and cry, "I can't take this anymore!" That worn-down, overwhelmed, helpless frustration — that is what it feels like to be exasperated.

Three things almost always go together with exasperation:

Intensity — it's not mild irritation; it's strong, heavy frustration.
Repetition — it usually builds up over time, caused by something that keeps happening.
Helplessness — there's often a sense that you can't easily escape or fix the cause.
How the Verb Works in a Sentence

Exasperate is a transitive verb, meaning it always needs an object — someone who receives the feeling. Something (or someone) does the exasperating, and a person experiences it.

The basic pattern: [cause] exasperates [person]

  • His constant interruptions exasperate his coworkers.
  • The slow internet exasperates me every time I try to work.
  • She exasperates her parents by never listening.

You can also flip it using passive voice:

  • I am exasperated by his endless complaints.
  • We were exasperated by the repeated delays.
The Three Related Forms You'll Encounter Constantly

These all come from the same root and you will see them everywhere, so knowing them is essential.

Exasperated is an adjective that describes how the person receiving the feeling looks or feels. She let out an exasperated sigh — meaning her sigh showed she was fed up. He gave me an exasperated look — his face said "I've had enough."

Exasperating is an adjective that describes the thing or person causing the feeling. His habit of arriving late is truly exasperating — the habit itself is what drives people crazy. What an exasperating situation!

Exasperation is the noun — it names the feeling itself, the emotion as a thing. She threw her hands up in exasperation. He spoke with barely concealed exasperation. There was a note of exasperation in her voice.
How It Differs from Words That Seem Similar

Several words live in the same neighborhood as exasperate, but each has its own shade of meaning.

Annoy is milder and more general. A single small incident can annoy you. Exasperation usually requires more build-up — it's annoyance that has been compounded and intensified.

Irritate is similar to annoy — it describes a surface-level, often mild reaction. It doesn't carry the sense of being pushed to one's limit the way exasperate does.

Frustrate is the closest cousin, but there's a key difference in direction. Frustration is mostly about being blocked — you want to reach a goal, but something stands in your way. Exasperation is more emotional and interpersonal — it's about being pushed past your limit, often by another person's behavior, not just an obstacle.

Infuriate is stronger and tilts heavily toward anger. If exasperation is "I can't take this anymore — WHY?!", infuriation is "I am furious." Exasperation carries more of a tired, worn-out quality; infuriation carries more heat.
The Emotional Texture — What Makes It Unique

This is the detail that really locks the word in place. Exasperation is not pure anger. It's also not sadness. It lives in a very specific emotional spot — the feeling you get when you say "Oh, come ON!" or "Why does this keep happening?!"

It's a cocktail of frustration + weariness + helplessness. You're not just mad — you're also tired of being mad, and you feel like nothing you do will change it. That three-part mix is what separates exasperate from every other similar word.
A Paragraph That Ties It All Together

Read this slowly and notice all four forms:

The student's repeated failure to submit homework exasperated the teacher, who left the room in pure exasperation, muttering, "Why does this keep happening?" It was, by any measure, an exasperating situation — and the teacher went home that evening feeling completely exasperated.

Verb → adjective for the person → noun → adjective for the situation → adjective for the person again. One word, four forms, one paragraph. That's the full picture.
